rule: Default block goal = the focus test with the lowest % of its benchmark target (biggest raw % gap).
summary: No study tests this rule directly. The nearest evidence, training aimed at an individual's force-velocity deficit, began with a positive trial; a later RCT in national-level athletes and a 2025 meta-analysis found no clear benefit over standard training, so 'attack the biggest deficit' is plausible but unproven. Reviews support building strength when an athlete is in a strength-deficit phase. A specific flaw: raw '% of target' is not comparable across tests. A 5% gap in threshold pace is far larger than a 5% gap in pull-ups (typical error 2% vs 10%), so the rule is biased toward noisy, fast-moving tests. Proposed: Rank gaps in comparable units: gap% / goal_change_pct (blocks needed to close), ignore gaps smaller than typical_error_pct, and break ties by athlete priority or race calendar. Fallback only; Claude still proposes with a stated trade-off. Bump the CODE_RULES version. Possibly wrong if: the normalized rule picks goals the athlete rejects more often than the current rule does.

sources.note: Jimenez-Reyes 2017: deficit-targeted (F-V) training improved jump height more consistently than generic training.
Lindberg 2021: training toward, away from or irrespective of the F-V deficit gave no group differences in athletes.
Solberg 2025: optimized F-V training corrects profiles, but jump gains are comparable to non-optimized training; unclear superiority.
Strength deficit, association and reserve phases: training emphasis depends on which phase the athlete is in.
